semantically_equivalent_domains.justification: Neuromodulation and neurostimulation are often used interchangeably in some contexts, both involving the alteration of nerve activity through targeted delivery of a stimulus.

parent_domains.justification: Neuromodulation is a branch within neuroscience, specifically focusing on the regulation and control of nervous system activity.

closest_parent_domain.justification: As neuromodulation involves altering processes within the nervous system, neuroscience serves as the broadest and most directly related domain.

child_domains.justification: Neuroergonomics can be a sub-domain of neuromodulation as it involves the understanding and application of brain function modulation to improve human-machine interaction.

closest_child_domain.justification: Neuroergonomics focuses on the application of neuroscience findings (including neuromodulation) to design work environments, making it closely related semantically.

sibling_domains.justification: Both clinical neurophysiology and neuromodulation involve the study and application of nervous system functions, with clinical neurophysiology offering diagnostic support for neuromodulation.
While computational neuroscience uses models and simulations, neuromodulation uses direct intervention, both aim to understand brain functions.
Cognitive neuroscience, like neuromodulation, examines brain functions, albeit through different perspectives and methodologies.

closest_sibling_domain.justification: Clinical neurophysiology closely relates to neuromodulation as it provides essential baseline understanding and measurement to facilitate targeted interventions in neuromodulation.

unrelated_domains.justification: Neuroanatomy focuses on the structure and organization of the nervous system, which is more static and less involved in the functional modulation aspect.
Brain structure studies the physical aspects rather than functional alterations that neuromodulation would focus on.
